title: Tenali and the Persian Horse Trader

full_text:
A cunning horse trader from the north arrived at the gates of Vijayanagara with a sleek, glossy black mare. He brought the steed before King Krishnadevaraya, who had an immense passion for fine warhorses.

'Jahanpanah!' praised the trader with extravagant flourishes. 'This is no ordinary mare. She was bred in the windswept plains of Bactria, sired by the desert storm! She is so swift that she does not touch the grass when galloping, and she runs faster than the autumn wind itself! I offer her to your royal cavalry for the modest price of five thousand gold dinars.'

The King was dazzled by the mare's gleaming coat and spirited posture. He was on the verge of ordering the treasurer to pay the five thousand gold coins when Tenali Raman stepped forward.

'Maharaj,' said Tenali, 'if this magnificent beast is truly swifter than the autumn wind, we must witness her celestial speed before the entire city! Let the trader mount her and demonstrate her wind-like flight around the royal polo grounds.'

The trader, whose horse had merely been fed sweet molasses and polished with oil to look energetic, began to sweat:
'Noble courtier, such a divine mare does not run on common dirt tracks for entertainment; she runs only when her spirit is moved by destiny!'

Tenali smiled innocently:
'Ah, then we shall assist destiny! Let me prepare the testing track!'
Tenali ran into the palace kitchens and returned carrying a small clay pot filled with freshly ground, pungent red chili powder and dried ginger.
He walked behind the mare, stroked her flank gently, and whispered:
'Let us see if she can outrun her own shadow!'

Tenali suddenly blew a small pinch of chili powder into the air near the horse's nostrils, while waving a burning bundle of aromatic lemongrass.
The mare sneezed violently, bucked with fright, and bolted forward!
The trader, trying desperately to mount her to save his reputation, grabbed the reins. The terrified horse leaped, dragging the trader through a muddy ditch, through a patch of prickly cactus, and finally dumping him headfirst into a heap of damp cow manure!

The horse trotted quietly to the royal stables to drink from the water trough, showing no magical speed whatsoever.
The King and the entire court erupted in uncontrollable laughter as the trader crawled out of the manure heap, his fine silk coat ruined and his pride shattered.

King Krishnadevaraya realized how close he had come to throwing away five thousand gold coins on empty boasting:
'Tenali, thy ginger and chili test has saved our treasury from a grand fraud!'
The trader was escorted out of the city gates, learning that in Vijayanagara, empty words cannot outrun practical wit.
moral: Impulsive vanity makes easy prey for swindlers; practical proof quickly exposes boastful claims.

Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
